analysis.one_liner: Gives individuals and businesses an optional 19% flat tax that ends after two years, and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor; it sat in the Ways and Means Committee until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let any individual or business permanently switch out of the normal income tax into a flat tax: 19% for the first two years, then 17%. The flat tax only applies to wages, retirement payouts, and unemployment benefits, so investment income like capital gains, dividends, and interest would go untaxed, and all existing tax credits, including the Child Tax Credit and Earned Income Tax Credit, would disappear. It would also repeal the federal estate, gift, and inheritance taxes entirely, and it would take a two-thirds vote in both chambers ever to raise the rate or shrink the deductions.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners and wealthy families gain the most. A household living off capital gains, dividends, and interest would pay nothing on that income after electing in, because the flat tax only counts wages and retirement distributions. Businesses gain a 19% rate (falling to 17%) on active business income with full deductions for inputs and wages, replacing the 21% corporate rate and higher individual rates. Heirs of large estates gain from the full repeal of the estate tax. Low-wage workers would lose more than they gain, since the flat tax strips away the refundable credits that erase or reverse their tax bills.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, businesses, and wealthy heirs

how_it_helps.text: Individuals may make a one-way election to pay 19% on taxable income for two years and 17% thereafter, in place of the regular income tax rates and the alternative minimum tax.

Flat-tax income counts only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, minus a standard deduction, so capital gains, dividends, and other investment income would not be taxed at all under the new regime.

Businesses electing the flat tax pay 19% (then 17%) on business income after deducting the full cost of inputs, wages, and retirement contributions, and they may not be subject to the corporate or individual income tax on that activity.
The bill repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for deaths and gifts after December 31, 2020.

Raising the flat tax rate or reducing the standard deduction or business deductions would require a two-thirds vote of both the House and Senate, making future rate increases far harder than ordinary legislation.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary taxpayers and the Treasury bear the cost. Wage earners who elect in lose every existing tax credit, including the Child Tax Credit and the Earned Income Tax Credit, which many low- and middle-income families rely on to cut or eliminate their federal tax bill. Because most high-income households have large investment income that the flat tax ignores, wealthy taxpayers would overwhelmingly elect in, shrinking federal revenue and leaving the remaining burden on households whose income is wages. The estate tax repeal also shifts inheritance taxation away from the largest estates.

drawbacks.text: Electing taxpayers lose all tax credits, which would raise taxes on many low- and working-income families who currently owe nothing or receive refunds through the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit.

Because the flat tax taxes only wages and retirement payouts, households with most of their income from investments would pay at or near zero, so the optional structure would tend to shift the tax burden toward people who work for a living.

The bill would cut federal revenue through lower rates, the exclusion of investment income, and full repeal of the estate and gift taxes, deepening deficits unless other taxes or spending cuts filled the gap, which the bill does not provide.
Requiring a two-thirds vote in both chambers to raise the rate or reduce deductions locks in the tax structure and makes ordinary majorities unable to adjust it later.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains flow to the top: untaxed investment income, a 17% rate on business profits, and no estate tax. The costs fall on the tax base that funds the government, and on low-income families who lose the credits that currently zero out their tax bills. The standard deduction is set high enough to spare some low-wage filers, but the loss of refundable credits and the revenue hole are serious design problems the bill does not address.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Rules Committee the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever held a hearing or sent it to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess introduced the Flat Tax Act on February 15, 2021, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Rules Committee.
No cosponsors ever signed on; the bill had zero cosponsors for its entire two-year life.
The only action after referral was a request for executive comment in October 2021; the bill never received a markup, a floor vote, or any consideration in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy households, large businesses, and big estates are better off because the bill died: the current system still taxes their investment income, corporate profits, and inheritances. Wage earners and the Treasury avoided the revenue loss and credit repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy households, businesses, and the Treasury

for.name: Rep. Michael C. Burgess
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Flat Tax Act on February 15, 2021 and recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; never held a markup or reported it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the partisan split was never tested; the sponsor was a Republican and the bill died quietly in a committee controlled by House Democrats.

industries.note: The flat tax would exempt capital gains, dividends, and interest entirely and cut rates on wages to 17%, and the estate tax repeal would end taxation of the largest inheritances. The revenue and the credit losses fall on everyone else.

Electing businesses would pay 17% (after two years at 19%) on income after full deductions for inputs, wages, and retirement contributions, replacing the 21% corporate rate. The cut comes out of federal revenue that funds public services.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth management services
industries.note: Repeal of the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes removes the tax planning those services exist to manage for very large estates.

The bill would impose a 17% employer tax on noncash benefits (like health coverage) provided to employees of tax-exempt organizations and governments, a new cost for those employers not borne in the current system.
